opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest thing is that benchmarks are, almost by construction, the tasks that are easy to measure, and the tasks that are easy to measure aren't necessarily the tasks that people actually care about. When you build a benchmark, you need a question with a clean, checkable answer. A multiple-choice question, a unit test that passes or fails, a number at the end of a math problem. But most of what I actually do in a day, and what most people do in their jobs, doesn't look like that at all. It's messy and underspecified, and half the work is figuring out what the question even is.

So you end up with this gap. A model can score incredibly well on some benchmark, and then you sit down and try to use it for something real and it falls over in a way the benchmark never would have predicted. And sometimes it goes the other direction, which I think people talk about less. A model will do badly on a benchmark, but when I actually use it, it's enormously helpful, because the thing that makes it useful to me isn't something anyone thought to put in a test.

The second concern is saturation and contamination. Benchmarks have a shelf life. Once a benchmark is published, it becomes a target, and as soon as it's a target, people optimize for it, sometimes deliberately and sometimes just because the data leaks into training sets from the internet. So you get these numbers going up and up, and it's really hard to tell how much of that is real capability and how much is the model having effectively seen something like the test before. We went through this with a whole series of benchmarks that were supposed to last years and got saturated in months.

And the third thing, which I care about a lot from a security perspective, is that benchmarks measure average-case performance, when what matters for a lot of real deployments is worst-case behavior. If a model gets 95% on some task, that sounds great, but if the 5% of failures are catastrophic, or if an adversary can reliably push you into that 5%, then the 95% isn't the number you should be looking at. Real-world tasks are often long chains of steps, too, so a small error rate per step compounds into a model that basically never finishes the whole thing correctly.

So what I've ended up doing, and what I'd honestly recommend to people, is to not trust the headline numbers very much and instead build your own small set of tasks that reflect what you actually need. Literally keep a list of things you've asked models to do that they couldn't do, and every time a new model comes out, try them again. It's not rigorous in the academic sense, but it tells you far more about whether a model will help you than any leaderboard will.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts easy-to-measure benchmarks with messy tasks people care about, but does not identify a mismatch between testing what humans find difficult and what real-world tasks require.

r002.rationale: It notes that errors compound across long chains of steps, but does not advocate evaluating models on tasks end to end.

r003.rationale: It says a model can score well on benchmarks yet fail in real use, and that a model with poor benchmark results can still be helpful in practice, describing a reversal between benchmark and real-world performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that worries me most is that benchmarks are, almost by construction, measuring the wrong thing, and we sort of know this and then forget it the moment a number comes out.

A benchmark is a proxy. You take some task you actually care about, like "can this model write code that solves a real problem for a real person," and you can't measure that directly, so you build a stand-in. You collect a few hundred problems, you write a grader, you get a number. And the problem is that the moment that number exists, people optimize for the number and not for the thing the number was supposed to stand in for. That's Goodhart's law, it's not a new observation, but it hits especially hard with language models because they're so good at pattern matching to whatever is in the training distribution.

The concrete thing that I keep running into is contamination, and not just the obvious kind where the test set literally ends up on the internet and gets scraped. That happens, and it's bad, but the subtler version is that the kinds of problems that make good benchmark questions are the kinds of problems that get written about a lot. They're self-contained, they have a clean answer, they're the sort of thing that shows up in textbooks and on Stack Overflow and in blog posts. So a model can get very good at exactly that shape of problem without that generalizing to the messy, underspecified, "the bug is actually in a config file three directories away" kind of task that constitutes most real work.

I've actually spent a lot of time on this with my own usage. I keep a running list of things I've actually asked models to do for me, real things, where I wanted the output and used it, and I look at how well they do on that versus how the benchmarks say they should do. And the correlation is there, it's not zero, but it's a lot noisier than the leaderboard would suggest. Models that are a few points apart on a coding benchmark can feel very different to use, and sometimes the one that's lower on the benchmark is the one I'd rather have.

The other thing that concerns me is the adversarial framing, which is where I come from. When I evaluate a defense in security, I'm not asking "does this work on the test set," I'm asking "what's the worst case." And benchmarks are essentially average-case measurements. A model that gets 85 percent might be failing on exactly the 15 percent that matters most, the cases that are unusual or high stakes, and the aggregate number hides that completely. If you're deploying something in the real world, the tail is what hurts you, and we almost never measure the tail.

And then the last thing is just that the tasks are too short. Most benchmarks are "here is a problem, produce an answer." Real tasks are "here is a vague goal, go figure out what the problem even is, make some decisions, realize you were wrong, back up, try again." The ability to do the first thing seems to be a necessary but really not sufficient condition for the second, and we are mostly measuring the first.

So I'm not saying throw out benchmarks, they're useful for tracking progress, they're useful for catching regressions. But I think people should treat them as a lower bound on how much you don't understand about the model, rather than as a measurement of what it can do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clean, self-contained benchmark problems with messy, underspecified real work, identifying a mismatch between benchmark tests and real-world task demands.

r002.rationale: It says real tasks involve figuring out the problem, making decisions, correcting mistakes, and trying again, and that benchmarks mostly measure short answer production. This supports evaluating models on the full task process.

r003.rationale: It says benchmark rankings can differ from which model the speaker prefers in personal use, but does not specifically describe performance reversing on agentic tasks.

astra-6.text:
One thing that concerns me is the gap between doing well on a benchmark and being useful at the task the benchmark is supposed to represent. We take something messy, like writing software or doing research, and turn it into a question with a clean answer that we can score automatically. That makes measurement easier, but it can remove a lot of what makes the real task difficult.

In practice, you have to figure out what the problem is, gather the right information, notice when you've made a mistake, and decide whether the result is actually good enough. A benchmark often hands you the problem and then checks the final answer. So a model can improve on that measure without improving equally on the whole process.

And reliability matters. If a model solves a task once in a hundred attempts, that's evidence it has some ability to do it. But if I need to inspect a hundred outputs to find the one that works, that may not save me any time. I'd like evaluations to tell us more about that: how much human help is required, how often the system succeeds, and whether we can recognize its failures.

r001.rationale: It contrasts clean, automatically scored questions with messy real tasks that require problem definition, information gathering, error detection, and judging quality.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks may miss the whole process and calls for evaluations that reveal human help required, success frequency, and whether failures can be recognized.

r003.rationale: It does not say that models’ relative rankings on benchmark test sets can reverse on agentic tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry about the gap between doing well on a benchmark and being useful on the task we actually care about. A benchmark takes some messy real-world activity and turns it into something we can score. That’s necessary, but you can lose a lot in that translation.

Take computer security. Finding a vulnerability in a small piece of code, when you’ve been told there’s a vulnerability there, is very different from being handed a large codebase and asked to find something important. In the real world, you have to decide where to look, pursue ideas that often go nowhere, and figure out whether what you found actually matters. Getting the answer right on a narrowly specified problem measures only part of that.

And then there’s reliability. A model can produce a really impressive result occasionally, but if someone has to spend hours checking every result, that changes how useful it is. I want evaluations that capture that whole process: how much help the model needs, how often it succeeds, and how much work a person has to do afterward. The benchmark score is evidence, but we should be careful about what we conclude from it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts narrow benchmark problems with the broader real-world task, but does not identify a mismatch involving what humans find difficult.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls for evaluations that capture the whole process, including assistance needed, success rate, and human follow-up work.

r003.rationale: It does not say that relative model performance can reverse between benchmark test sets and agentic tasks.
